messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
Here's a ~250-word opening for a blog post on observability:

---

A service goes down at 2 a.m. The on-call engineer wakes up, opens a dashboard, and stares at a wall of green checkmarks that mean nothing. CPU is fine. Memory is fine. Somewhere underneath those metrics, a queue is backing up and nobody can see it.

This is the gap observability exists to close. Monitoring tells you a system is unhealthy; observability tells you why. The difference matters more as systems get harder to reason about. A monolith with one database is easy to debug by intuition — you've read the code, you know where things break. A fleet of microservices calling each other across networks, retrying, timing out, and failing in combinations nobody predicted is a different problem. No engineer holds that whole picture in their head, so the system itself has to be able to answer questions it wasn't built to anticipate.

That's the real test of observability: not whether you have dashboards, but whether you can ask a question you didn't know you'd need to ask — "which requests are slow, and what do they have in common?" — and get an answer from the data you already collected. Logs, metrics, and traces are the raw material. Observability is what you get when they're connected well enough to trace a single request end to end.

Teams that invest here don't just cut their time to resolution. They change how confidently they ship, because they're no longer flying blind between deploys and the next incident.
